questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to explore the Mexican culture both for academic and personal reasons. I felt that the culture would be a great counter point to the Danish mentality, maybe teaching me important life lessons about enjoying life and being a bit more present and taking things a bit more calmly. At the same time, I wanted to explore a completely different culture, and thought that choosing a country in the Latin America countries, a region that soon the EU will colaborate a lot with, could be helpful for my future career.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Mexico really is an absolutely amazing country! So incredibly rich in culture.. The food, the beautiful colored buildings, walking around in a pastel heaven sipping on a fresh juice smoothie. Mexico is amazing. Understanding the diversity of this country has been one of most rewarding experiences of my stay. At the end of the stay, you will most likely have visited way more places in Mexico than the average Mexican - most Mexicans don't even get to visit another state in their life. In this way, it is very priviliged to get a chance to have 5 months to explore this hugely rich cultural place.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UDLAP sends a lot of infomation and the exchange office are super helpful - Eduardo is a darling!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Some long PDFs explaining how to get to the airport, what to bring, what not to bring. It was all very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I arrived late, so when I came I didn't even know how to log in on the students portal blackboard to see my homework. But maybe I should have been more conscious of that and have asked for help - it was just hard knowing what to ask for without having been given any information. If you arrive late, I would advice you to simply pop by the international office and ask them to help you understand the system - especially if you, like me, don't speak Spanish!

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy. There are a lot of housing groups. The big ones are: Cholula Capital, Charro Housing, Travels Life, Si Senor. In this order from more to less, they are focused on parties.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is so different in Cholula to any other exchange city I have ever heard about. All of the beforementioned housing companies litterally feed off exchange students; they cater to them by arranging weekly salsa nights (Tuesday), techno nights (Wednesday), parties Thursday in the big clubs and house parties in the weekend. In this way, you never have to be bored. At the same time, it was a bit unappealing to me how everything worked. A lot of the men running these companies hook up with the young girls who make use of these companies services, and there is a lot of very youthful drinking culture going on (think A LOT of drinking games) which to a Danish person can seem a bit off-putting and remind you more of high school than of a university experience.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The international housing is cheap, and I don't know many other options. If you can live with locals, I think it would make for a more interesting stay. Also; many of the international students have never lived alone or cooked for themselves before, so expect that your kitchen will be a complete and utter mess if you choose to live in international housing. In this case you kind of have to accept that you will not be able to cook in your own kitchen, and rely on take-away tacos and snacks from Oxxo instead.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Quite easy, but a bit annoyingly bureaucratic. You had to both fill out a form and send a list of your choices to the coordinator.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always ask the international office.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got every single one I wanted - I got a feeling that they were very flexible with helping you, and that you shouldn't worry too much about not getting your courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't worry too much about it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic isn't very very high, but the system is so different than in Denmark. Here, you are being graded on a mix of points made from assignments, presentations, final exams, ect. You need to get more than 80 points out of a 100 to pass at master's level. For me, this meant that the work load was much much higher than in Denmark, and I actually ended up studying from morning til night most of my days at UDLAP to keep up with the work. Which is interesting, because most students at master's level are grown ups with full time jobs who studies at the site - so all my courses (which were two times two hours a week - in total four hours of class pr week) were held at night from 18-20.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had master's courses in Spanish even though I don't speak Spanish. It is not as fun, of course, to sit in class, but since many readings are in English, I still have learned a lot from writing my assignments, which my teachers agreed for me to do in English.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As mentioned before, very few class hours but a lot of time consuming assignments - at least one pr course pr week.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Governance and Political Theory
Global Political Economy
Regional Studies
International Studies and Institutions

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Global Political Economy was really interesting, and the professors slides are in English, which made it way easier for me to follow his class. Regional Studies have an unproportional big workload, so I wouldn't recommend that course unless you want to study all your wake hours your last weeks of your exchange.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Mobile data is expensive I would recommend that you buy a subscribtion from the beginning on instead of ordering new data all the time from Telcel like I did - this way is flexible and telcel is a stable network, but it is way too expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Regular groceries in the supermarkets are not that much cheaper than in Denmark. Oats are more expensive, milk is the same, eggs only a bit cheaper. Eating out at every meal will almost cost you the same as cooking home-cooked meals.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of different things! Photography, dance and music classes, sports.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I took ballet three times a week from 8-9 am. I didn't show up to most classes, as it simply was too early for me to get a good nights sleep if I didn't want to go to bed early most days. If I could do it all over, I would focus more on learning the dances of Latin America and maybe sign up for salsa in Cholula instead of at UDLAP.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I went to the north, where there really was nothing to see. On the other hand, it was fascinating to escape the tourists routes and really meet the real Mexico, and in that way, it is one of the experiences I remember the most clearly. Travelling with some of the international housing and travel companies are cheap and accesable ways to get around and seeing a lot in a few days, but the bus rides are very exhausting, and there is often a lot of focus on drinking.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Not hard at all. Mexicans are very nice. I found it harder to adjust to the culture of many of the international students, who would be quite young and focus mostly on cheating on their partners back home and drinking. Cholula is a place where party is big, so you kind of need to make up your mind if you want to take part of that whole international party scene and mostly hang out with internationals, or try to seek out a bit more local experiences.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just meet them at parties. There are a lot of really really cool locals whom it is nice to befriend.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: many people talk about the male "machismo" but I want to shout out that almost all Mexican men I was introduced to were very respectful and progressive - with a few exceptions. Men can be very insisting here, and walking in the streets outside of Cholula, you shouldn't let your guard down completely. Being in Mexico City alone as a woman was a big eye-opener to the constant sexism and unsafety facing women in Mexico. I went to the women's march on 8 March, and we were told to write down telephone numbers on our skin in case it got violent and something happened to us. Kidnappings also happens here, even in Cholula, so even though I didn't feel too unsafe in this little town, you still need to be careful. A french exhange student got kidnapped and had her nose broken last semester.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I mostly appreciated the diversity of the culture of the different states in Mexico. The richness of the different foods, costumes, costoms, beliefs - it is just overwhelming how much there is to do, learn and see here!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
You are never going to see rugbrød during your 5 months here. Yesterday, I dreamt that a Mexican friend gave me rugbrød as a surprise present. Embrace it though, you will soon be home again. 
Bring: a good book. There are very few options for finding English speaking books, so buy your lonely planet - Mexico beforehand or buy it in Amazon. 
Also something surprising; the fashion is so different in Mexico, so don't except to buy your summer wardrobe while you are here - bring clothes you like with you from back home. I got one of my bras ruined while it was being washed, and it took me two months to find a reasonably pretty bra without padding here in Mexico. Padding is big here, and most clothes are fast fashion made of plastic materials - and not even that cheap either! 
So bring;
- clothes you like (clubbing clothes too, as you will most likely go out a lot)
- rugbrød
- a warm sweater, as the weather changes a lot. You don't need your heavy leather boots or leather jacket though - I would think more in layers when I was packing.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The stay at UDLAP is a bit like a prison sometimes. You have to show your ID card when you enter and exit campus, when you want to enter the library and even when you want to buy lunch! Security is such a big thing in Mexico, and since UDLAP is a private university, parents expect high leves of security. Also; except that the Mexicans you will meet at UDLAP will come from the very priviliged parts of Mexican society. They are still lovely all of them though!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The richness of the culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The international students being quite young and wanting to party like in Danish high schools. But for sure you can choose a different kind of stay if this doesn't appeal to you. And if it does; enjoy!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
